3. Full Sovereign Guarantee (FSG) Model. This document describes a Full Sovereign Guarantee (FSG) structure in which host governments provide a sovereign guarantee covering 100% of each city's $306.25B construction cost while Delper builds, owns, and operates 100% of all 5,000 acres. No sovereign guarantee agreements, MDB commitments, or government approvals have been signed or committed to by any government or multilateral institution.

4. Urban Reclamation & Retrofitting Programme (Phase 4). This document introduces a new Phase 4 programme: Retrofitting and Urban Reclamation of legacy cities vacated after populations are relocated to completed smart cities. Each reclaimed city is estimated at USD 306.5B in retrofit cost with a 5-year build timeline and USD 30.65B/yr in revenue commencing from Year 6 of each project, being 10% per annum on the total USD 306.5B investment. This is the sole revenue stream per retrofit city — no separate operational revenue is counted in addition to this 10% yield. Across 2,200 retrofit cities at terminal state: USD 67.43T/yr total retrofit revenue · USD 47.201T/yr net profit at 70% margin. Capital is raised through issuance of Medium Term Notes (MTNs) backed by completed smart cities as collateral with 100% sovereign guarantee, issued at 3% per annum for 25-year tenor to FIIs, retired by Year 20 at USD 153,300/year per note, in denominations of USD 200,000 and integral multiples of USD 1,000. No MTNs have been issued. No reclamation projects have commenced. All reclamation figures are illustrative forward-looking projections.

15. Debt Payoff Process. This document describes a debt payoff mechanism under which 2,200 operational smart cities — each employing 2 million workers at $200,000/month per worker — generate a combined monthly revenue of $880T and annual net profit of $2,112T. Under full reinvestment (100% profit allocation with cascade effect), the total debt stack of $1,332.41T is projected to be fully cleared by Year 16.1 (Month 74), leaving a surplus reinvestment pool of $6,059.59T (4.5× the total debt). Each city batch clears its own share of debt within approximately 7.6 months of becoming operational, then reinvests its surplus. The cascade effect of sequential batch activation compresses total payoff to mid-Year 16. Post-payoff, all $2,112T/yr annual profit is available for free reinvestment into further city expansion, humanitarian programmes, and token buybacks. These debt payoff projections are illustrative forward-looking statements only. No debt has been incurred. No repayment schedule has been agreed with any lender.

The Full Sovereign Guarantee — Why This Changes Everything
In the prior PPP model, Delper ceded 25% of each city to the government in exchange for a 25% sovereign guarantee. In the Full Sovereign Guarantee (FSG) Model, Delper invests and builds 100% of all 5,000 acres — retaining 100% ownership, 100% rental income, and 100% control — while the host government provides a 100% sovereign guarantee on the full city construction cost of $306.25B. This is not a traditional PPP: the government contributes no land, no construction capital, and no operational resource. The government's sole contribution is its sovereign creditworthiness — a guarantee letter backed by national treasury. In exchange, Delper builds a complete smart city that generates $5.36B/yr in tax revenues, provides $247/month to every resident, eliminates urban unemployment, and eliminates the government's housing and food subsidy burden entirely. The government gets the greatest urban development in history at zero CapEx. Delper gets 100% ownership backed by the AAA/AA rating of the host sovereign — enabling SBLC financing at 1.5–2.0% versus 4.5–5.5% commercial. This is the world's first sovereign-guaranteed private city programme at scale.
Delper (GK Bharta) Builds 100% of all 5,000 acres. Operates all city systems. Deploys all 7 Claude AI agents. Installs all quantum infrastructure. Provides $247/month to 2.5M residents. 100% ownership of the completed city ($306.25B asset). 100% of rental income ($21.44B/yr per city). Full control of DPR token economy, supply chain fees, and digital revenue. GK Bharta retains the city in perpetuity — never sold. Construction execution risk. Cost overrun risk. Technology risk. These are managed by Delper's 7-layer quantum security, ASHE autonomous ops, and Agent 4 construction management. Restored to full 100% ownership vs 75% in prior PPP. Rental income restored to $21.44B/city/yr vs $16.08B. No land concession. No operational sharing. Full moat.
Host Government Issues a sovereign guarantee letter (equivalent to a treasury-backed SBLC counter-guarantee) covering 100% of the city's $306.25B construction cost. This is a contingent liability — only called if Delper defaults on the bank debt. Delper's rental income of $21.44B/yr on a $306.25B asset provides 13.1× DSCR coverage — default probability is near zero. A fully operational smart city housing 2.5M residents at zero CapEx to government. Elimination of housing shortage, unemployment, and urban poverty in the city's catchment area. $5.36B/yr estimated tax revenue from city economic activity. No ongoing SBLC fee, no construction management burden, no technology investment required. Contingent sovereign credit risk: if Delper defaults (probability near zero given 13.1× DSCR), the sovereign must cover the outstanding bank debt. Sovereign's risk is mitigated by: Delper's IAH token system, ACRE breach reversal, quantum security, and the city asset itself (which the sovereign could operate as fallback). Prior PPP required govt to build 25% zone ($76.25B construction) + manage civic operations. FSG requires zero CapEx from govt — only a signature on a guarantee letter. Governments in 60 jurisdictions overwhelmingly prefer FSG.
SBLC / MDB Banks Issue construction financing against the sovereign guarantee. No longer evaluating Delper's commercial risk alone — they are lending against the sovereign credit of the host government. ADB, World Bank, AIIB, AfDB, IDB, IsDB, EBRD can now fund the FULL $306.25B per city (not just 25%) at sovereign window rates. Sovereign-quality infrastructure loan at 1.5–2.0% rate. Interest income on $306.25B/city × 2,200 cities = $673.75T total lending portfolio over programme life. Single largest sovereign infrastructure lending programme in MDB history. Recurring relationship: each city generates 25+ years of interest income. Sovereign credit risk of host government — typically AA/A rated. Far lower risk than commercial city developer risk. MDB co-guarantee (ADB partial guarantee, World Bank MIGA) further reduces bank credit exposure to near-zero for the MDB-covered 573 cities. Prior structure: commercial SBLC on 75% + MDB sovereign on 25% = blended 3.2% rate. FSG: sovereign guarantee on 100% = 1.8% blended rate. Saving: 1.4% on $306.25B/city = $4.29B/city/yr during construction. Across 2,200 cities: $9.43T/yr peak financing saving.

Full Sovereign Guarantee Model — Delper Builds 100% · Government Guarantees 100% · Transformative Capital Structure

Part B · SBLC Bank Jurisdiction Matrix · Full Sovereign Guarantee (FSG) Model
"We don't want to risk our sovereign balance sheet" The contingent liability is covered by the city's own rental income at 13.1× DSCR. The sovereign guarantee is only callable if Delper fails to service debt — which requires rental income to fall below 1.25× debt service on a $21.44B/yr income stream. This has never occurred in any income-producing city asset globally. The guarantee is a signature, not a cash outlay. India's sovereign guarantee for NHAI highway bonds. UAE sovereign guarantee for Dubai World infrastructure. Saudi Arabia's PIF guarantees for NEOM. All provided on income-producing infrastructure with near-zero call probability.
"What do we get in exchange?" A complete 5,000-acre smart city housing 2.5M of their citizens at zero government CapEx. $247/month to every resident — eliminating urban poverty in one transaction. Zero rent, zero food cost for 2.5M people. Estimated $5.36B/yr in tax revenues from city economic activity. 50,000–200,000 city jobs in construction and operations. All at the cost of a guarantee letter. Ningbo Smart City (China): government guarantee unlocked $18B in private investment. Lusaka Smart City (Zambia): sovereign guarantee enabled $4.2B AfDB-backed construction at zero government CapEx outlay.
"We lose control of our territory" The FSG Concession Agreement grants Delper a 99-year operating concession — not a land sale. The government retains sovereignty, land title, and the right to revert the city to national ownership at end-concession. Residents are citizens of the host nation — not "Delper residents." The city operates under the host nation's legal system. DPR tokens are the internal economic medium but government taxes are collected in national currency via an agreed revenue-sharing formula. Dubai's Jebel Ali Free Zone: 50-year concession to private operator, UAE retains full sovereignty. Singapore's Jurong Island: private industrial operators on long-term concession, Singapore remains sovereign. UK's PFI: private operators run hospitals and schools under 30-year concessions on government-owned land.
"What if Delper fails?" If Delper were to fail (near-zero probability given 7-layer quantum security, $673.75T asset portfolio, $13.062T/yr net profit, and 6B users), the sovereign guarantee is called. The sovereign takes ownership of a completed $306.25B city generating $21.44B/yr rental income — a windfall for the government. The "downside" scenario is owning the world's most advanced smart city at zero net cost after rental income offsets debt service. This is structurally equivalent to airline leasing: if the airline fails, the lessor (bank) repossesses a revenue-generating asset. The sovereign is in the position of the lessor — the "default" upside is owning the asset.
"Our constitution prohibits sovereign guarantees for private entities" FSG Concession Agreement structured as a Public-Private Infrastructure Development Agreement (PPIDA) — the same legal vehicle used by World Bank and ADB for sovereign infrastructure co-investment. Government's role is reclassified as "infrastructure facilitation authority" not "guarantor for a private company." Legal counsel in each jurisdiction advises on specific structuring. Agent 2 (Regulatory Intelligence) maps the exact legal vehicle required per jurisdiction's constitutional framework. ADB's PPP project structuring in India, Philippines, Vietnam, and Indonesia has navigated identical constitutional constraints through PPIDA vehicles in all four jurisdictions.

SBLC Bridge — FSG-Enhanced Strategic Context

The SBLC Bridge is Delper's primary capital instrument in the FSG model — no longer just a contingency. Under the Full Sovereign Guarantee model, the SBLC is issued against the host government's sovereign creditworthiness, enabling construction financing at 1.5–2.0% versus 4.5–5.5% commercial. Under base-case projections, all 2,200 cities are funded through trade programme profits ($401.44T), IPO/FPO equity ($135T), and the DPR token pledge loan ($137.31T) — the FSG sovereign SBLC provides parallel low-cost debt that accelerates delivery by 3–5 years per city and reduces total financing cost by $9.43T/yr at peak construction. A callable Standby Letter of Credit (MT760 SWIFT, first-demand, unconditional) issued against the host government's sovereign guarantee backs each city's construction loan. On practical completion, the SBLC is replaced by the city asset itself ($306.25B valuation) and city rental revenue ($21.44B/city/yr) services the debt — the sovereign guarantee is released and never called.

Recommended First Step: Engage ADB + Standard Chartered Singapore + HSBC Singapore simultaneously for a tri-party term sheet on Batch 0 (50 cities, $15.3T CapEx at $306.25B/city) from Year 4, underpinned by sovereign guarantee letters from the 20 host governments in Batch 0's jurisdiction set.

Key Structural Protections for SBLC Lenders

  • Revenue assignment signed at drawdown — lender holds contractual claim on city rental income ($21.44B/city/yr) from construction close, not on completion.
  • Independent city valuation by Big-4 or specialist infrastructure valuer on practical completion — activates Phase 2 collateral transition.
  • DSCR covenant of 1.25× minimum — lender step-in rights trigger before any default. City NOI ($16.44B/yr) provides 13.1× DSCR coverage.
  • No government guarantee required — city asset + revenue stream is fully self-sufficient collateral.
  • SBLC from rated bank (BBB+/Baa1 minimum) is callable on first demand — unconditional and irrevocable.
  • $5.0T ESG Bond Programme (3.21% blended coupon, redeemed Y9–Y14) provides additional parallel liquidity channel.
  • GK Bharta promoter stake ($63.66T at Year 5 EV) available as additional security for anchor lender comfort — 7.8% LTV capacity of $4.96T.
  • Shadow ledger on Hyperledger Besu provides real-time, auditable rental income and city asset performance data to all lenders.

The Gap This Section Closes
Having 7 Claude agents defined is not the same as being able to build, deploy, and scale them in real time. This section defines Delper's complete GenAI runtime stack: how new agent capabilities are built and tested, how prompts are versioned and deployed without downtime, how inference is served at 70,000 QPS with sub-100ms latency, how RAG pipelines keep agents grounded in live city data, and how auto-scaling responds to demand spikes across 2,200 cities without manual intervention.
Prompt Registry PromptLayer + Anthropic Console Every system prompt for all 7 agents versioned, tagged, and immutably recorded. Rollback to any prior prompt version in <60 seconds. No live agent ever runs an unregistered prompt. 7 agents × 38 language variants = 266 prompt templates under version control
A/B Model Routing Anthropic API model aliases + LangChain Router New prompt or model version (e.g. Opus 4.7 candidate) routes 5% of traffic while current version handles 95%. Statistical significance tested before full cutover. Zero-downtime model upgrades across all 7 agents. Per-agent routing; city-level traffic split; jurisdiction-specific overrides
Context Window Management LangChain Memory + CockroachDB session store Agent 3 (KYC): 200K-token context window manages full merchant application in one pass. Agent 4 (City): context window carries full Gantt timeline + satellite analysis per city site. Redis caches hot context for sub-10ms retrieval. 200K tokens per Opus 4.6 session; Redis TTL 24h for active merchant sessions
System Prompt Integrity Hyperledger SHA-256 hash Every prompt hash recorded on-chain before execution. Prompt injection attempts (OWASP LLM01) detected by hash mismatch at inference gateway before reaching Claude API. Zero tolerance: any hash mismatch suspends agent and triggers F4 Class E incident response. Real-time hash verification at 70,000 QPS (Agent 5 baseline)

Layer 2 · Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — Live City Data into Every Agent

Primary Inference Gateway Anthropic API (direct) via Amazon AI Cloud VPC endpoint All 7 Claude agents call Anthropic API through a private VPC endpoint in each of 3 regional anchors (Singapore, Dubai, London). No public internet hop. Latency baseline: 18–35ms to Anthropic API from Amazon AI Cloud anchor. 3 regional anchors active-active; automatic failover <200ms; SLA 99.99%
Request Batching & Queue vLLM continuous batching + Apache Kafka queue Agent 5 (Risk) at 70,000 QPS: requests batched dynamically using vLLM PagedAttention to maximise GPU memory utilisation. Kafka queue absorbs burst spikes (up to 3× baseline for 90 seconds) without dropping requests or degrading latency. Burst capacity: 210,000 QPS for 90s; queue depth alert at 50,000 pending
Streaming Response Anthropic API streaming (SSE) + WebSocket relay Agent 3 (KYC merchant onboarding): streaming responses sent token-by-token to KYC reviewer UI — first token appears in <800ms, eliminating perceived latency for human reviewers. Agent 4 (City Management): streaming used for real-time Gantt update generation. Time-to-first-token <800ms for Opus 4.6; streaming throughout for multi-minute city analysis runs
NVIDIA Triton Inference Server NVIDIA Triton + TensorRT-LLM Auxiliary local models (embedding generation for RAG; classification guardrails; PII detection before Claude API call) run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs via Triton on Amazon AI Cloud. Reduces calls to Anthropic API by pre-filtering irrelevant or malicious inputs at the infrastructure layer. Embedding generation: <2ms per document; PII scan: <5ms; runs 24/7 in each regional anchor
Model Tier Auto-Routing LangChain Router + cost threshold policy Automatically routes tasks to cheapest capable model: Haiku 4.5 for classification and simple extraction; Sonnet 4.6 for structured analysis; Opus 4.6 for complex reasoning. Shadow Deployment New model version runs in shadow mode alongside production for minimum 48 hours: receives all real traffic, produces outputs, but outputs are not acted upon. DPIA Mandate: When Required Before Deployment

Under GDPR Article 35, a DPIA is mandatory before any processing that is likely to result in a high risk — including (a) systematic evaluation of persons using automated processing (Agents 1, 3, 5), (b) large-scale processing of special categories of data (Agent 3 — biometrics), and (c) systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area at large scale (Agent 4 — city infrastructure). DPIAs must be completed, reviewed by the DPO, and filed with the relevant supervisory authority before any live agent processing begins in EU-jurisdictions.

Why Proactive Data Governance Is Required
Processing biometric, financial, and location data for 6 billion residents across 60 jurisdictions is one of the largest personal data operations in human history. GDPR Article 35 mandates a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before any large-scale processing of biometric or sensitive data. India's DPDPA 2023, Brazil's LGPD, and Singapore's PDPA impose equivalent obligations. This section establishes Delper's proactive data governance framework — not merely a breach-response policy.

🏙️ The Urban Reclamation Thesis — Eliminating Ghost Towns · Creating Circular Asset Value

By transitioning from building new commercial smart cities to reclaiming existing mixed habitats, Delper eliminates the risk of leaving behind economically dead "ghost towns." Instead, the system transforms legacy urban centres into high-yield, automated corporate real estate networks under a PPP model. Every vacated legacy city becomes a new revenue-generating asset — backed by the same MTN and sovereign guarantee framework that funded the smart cities that replaced it. This is not urban sprawl: it is urban transformation at civilisational scale, creating a self-reinforcing circular economy where each completed smart city becomes the collateral for the next reclamation project.

Layer 1 · Elastic Edge Front-Ending Proxies · ∞ Auto-Scaling
Auto-scaling — infinite proxy nodes spin up/down dynamically with traffic. Dynamic IP rotation — no fixed IP signatures for attackers to target. SSL offloading — TLS 1.3 terminated at edge, traffic re-encrypted for upstream via mTLS. Every proxy instance issues a short-lived private certificate (TTL: 60 minutes, auto-rotated by HSM). Layer 2 · Strict Upstream Reverse-Proxy Sync · HTTP/2 + HTTP/3 Enforced
HTTP Request Smuggling eliminated — rigid protocol alignment across entire network topology. All edge proxies and back-end application layers communicate strictly via uniform HTTP/2 or binary HTTP/3 transport streams. No protocol downgrade permitted. Header validation enforced at every hop: missing or malformed headers trigger automatic request rejection and threat log event routed to Agentic AI Threat Layer.
▼ Private VPC Peering Loop Only ▼
Layer 3 · Deterministic Main Application · Zero Public Access · Strict Internal Auth
Zero public access points — the main application has no public IP. Only VPC-peered proxy nodes with valid mTLS certificates can reach it. Strict internal auth — every incoming packet must carry a verified internal signature. Packets without verification are instantly rejected — even if originating from within the local network cluster. The Agentic AI Threat Layer analyzes all authenticated requests before routing to the 16-module deterministic engine.

The Humanitarian Inversion — Platform Revenue Flows Down, Not Up
Every traditional platform extracts value from users. Delper inverts this: advertisers pay the platform, the platform passes $247/month to every resident, residents pay $0 rent (covered by Delper's rental surplus), and residents pay $0 for staple food (covered by the Food Sovereignty Programme). The 6 billion people who join Delper are not the product — they are the beneficiaries. The PPP model deepens this inversion: host governments contribute their 25% city zone as civic infrastructure (schools, health centres, emergency services), which Delper residents access at zero cost, funded by the sovereign partner's own rental income from that 25% zone. For the first time in history, a business model exists where every user of a $62.40T/yr platform receives more value than they pay for.

The Answer Is: Yes — And This Must Be Governed
Delper's quantum computer is not a request-response system like a Claude API call. The D-Wave quantum annealer and IBM/Google Willow hybrid run continuous, ambient optimisation across all 2,200 city nodes — processing city variables, energy loads, food logistics, and settlement data whether or not an explicit command was issued. This is by design: that continuous processing is what makes 2,200-city coordination possible. But it means the quantum layer is always reading and processing information far beyond any single prompt. Without a formal boundary policy, this creates three risks: data minimisation violations (GDPR Art. 5), undocumented AI decision-making (EU AI Act Art. 13), and regulatory exposure in jurisdictions that require purpose-specific data use. This section defines exactly what the quantum system processes, why, and what it is structurally prevented from doing.
City Resource Variables Energy load balancing, water distribution, waste routing, and construction sequencing across 2,200 cities must be solved as a single optimisation problem at sub-second cadence. Waiting for an explicit command would introduce multi-second delays incompatible with city-scale operations. D-Wave quantum annealer: continuous QUBO (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimisation) across all city nodes No — aggregate city metrics only; no resident-level data Data fed to annealer is pre-aggregated at city-node level; personal data structurally excluded at ingestion layer via Kafka filter
Blockchain Consensus Validation CRYSTALS-Dilithium PQC signatures must be verified at hardware level for every transaction at 50,000 TPS. Signature verification cannot be batched to a command — it runs inline with every block proposal across all 200 validator nodes. Quantum-native PQC verification: generates and verifies lattice-based signatures at hardware speed Transaction hash only — no plaintext personal data; wallet address is pseudonymous ZK-SNARK layer wraps transaction data before quantum layer sees it; quantum system processes cryptographic proofs, not underlying data
QKD Key Refresh Quantum Key Distribution between 3 regional anchors (Singapore, Dubai, London) requires continuous photon-entangled key generation. Keys are refreshed on a rolling basis, not on command — a stale key is a security vulnerability. Photonic QKD: continuous entangled photon pair generation and key material production between anchor sites No — cryptographic key material only; no content data QKD subsystem is physically air-gapped from all data planes; key material passed to HSM via hardware-only interface; no software access path
Fraud Pattern Ambient Scan (Agent 5 support) Agent 5 uses Grover's algorithm to pattern-match across 6B wallet transaction history. The quantum substrate maintains a continuously-updated index of flagged patterns so that when an explicit fraud query arrives at 70,000 QPS, the Grover search executes in microseconds rather than seconds. Grover's algorithm: maintains live amplitude-amplified search index over anonymised transaction pattern corpus Pattern corpus only — wallet addresses hashed; no names, biometrics, or KYC data in quantum layer Pattern corpus anonymised before quantum ingestion; re-identification structurally prevented by one-way hash; Agent 5 handles de-anonymisation only in classical layer after human-in-the-loop trigger

What the Quantum System Processes Only On Explicit Command — Strict Scope Boundaries

Biometric Data (facial templates, fingerprints) GDPR Article 9 special category. Quantum processing of biometric data without explicit consent and supervisory authority approval is a Category A violation. No optimisation task requires biometric data at quantum layer — all biometric decisions are made in the classical Sumsub pipeline. Kafka filter: any payload tagged biometric_data=true is routed exclusively to classical Sumsub API; quantum ingestion pipeline has no schema field for biometric data — it cannot receive it even if submitted GDPR Art. 9; India DPDPA Section 8; EU AI Act Art. 10 (training data prohibition)
Named Personal Identity Data (names, national IDs, passport numbers) Quantum optimisation requires only anonymous feature vectors. No city resource scheduling, fraud pattern, or financial optimisation task requires a person's name or ID number. Inclusion would constitute purpose limitation violation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)) — the quantum system has no lawful basis to process named individuals. Pre-quantum anonymisation layer: all data is hashed and de-identified before Kafka submits to quantum queue. Hash is one-way: quantum system cannot reverse it. Re-identification occurs only in classical layer, only when legally required, only under human authorisation. GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) purpose limitation; GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation; MAS PDPA Singapore
Unencrypted Financial Account Data (raw wallet balances, bank account numbers) Quantum computers are the primary long-term threat to RSA and ECC encryption. Storing unencrypted financial data in a system that also runs quantum algorithms would create an attack surface that undermines Delper's entire security architecture. This is a structural contradiction. Financial data in quantum layer exists only as ZK-SNARK proofs or CRYSTALS-Dilithium-signed hashes — never as plaintext. The quantum system can verify correctness of a transaction without ever seeing the underlying balance or account number. 7-Layer Hack-Proof Framework Layer 1; CRYSTALS-Dilithium mandate; F2 Section
Confidential Legal & SAR Data SAR filings, pending litigation, and legal opinions are subject to legal professional privilege and AML secrecy obligations in all 60 jurisdictions. Any quantum-layer access to this data would create discoverable evidence of system-level data commingling — a serious legal liability. Agent 1 and Agent 2 operate entirely in classical Hyperledger-secured environment. No interface exists between the quantum optimisation layer and the compliance data store. Physical network separation enforced: compliance DB is on a separate VLAN with no quantum API endpoint. FATF Recommendation 20 (SAR secrecy); legal professional privilege; AML Directive Article 39 (EU)
Resident Food & Welfare Entitlement Records Household food allocation and welfare data constitutes vulnerability-linked data under ICRC data protection standards and is treated as special category data in conflict-adjacent regions. Quantum processing would require Article 9 GDPR basis — no such basis exists for optimisation tasks. Agent 6 agronomy data enters the quantum layer only as anonymised crop yield aggregates at farm-cluster level. Individual household food entitlement records never leave the Agent 6 classical processing environment. Weaviate partition for Agent 6 has no quantum read endpoint. ✓  Audit trail: Every command-triggered quantum task is logged on Hyperledger with: task ID, submitting human identity, authorisation record, data class hash submitted, and quantum output hash. Retrievable within 30 minutes. Retained 7 years.

Why Scheduled Commands Matter
Ambient quantum processing keeps cities running moment-to-moment. Scheduled commands do something different: they recalibrate the entire system at defined intervals — rebalancing optimisation weights, refreshing cryptographic baselines, validating node integrity, and stress-testing the quantum mesh against current city count and load. Without a published schedule, there is no audit trail, no governance cadence, and no way for SBLC banks or regulators to verify the quantum system was operating within its defined parameters at any point in time. What Counts as a "Different Operations" Node
A standard city node joins the network with a predefined operations profile (residential, commercial, industrial mix). A node with different operations means: a city with a specialised economic zone (e.g. NEOM-type tech cluster), a humanitarian-only city (conflict-adjacent rebuild node), a quantum research hub node, a cross-border trade node spanning two jurisdictions, or any node whose QUBO variable set differs from the standard 2,200-city template. These nodes cannot simply inherit the standard configuration — the quantum optimisation layer must be explicitly reconfigured to handle their unique variable structure.
N1 Node Variable Profile Registration CTO submits the new node's QUBO variable schema — its unique combination of resource types, transaction classes, jurisdiction rules, and economic zone parameters. Quantum layer ingests the schema, validates it against the master 2,200-city variable library, and assigns the node a unique quantum namespace. Duplicate or conflicting variable definitions are rejected. Agent 4 (City Management), Agent 1 (jurisdiction compliance check), Hyperledger node registry Schema accepted with zero conflicts. If conflicts detected → CTO + CAIGO review; node cannot go live until resolved. Namespace assigned and published to Hyperledger within 4 hours of acceptance. CTO + CAIGO
N2 Quantum Mesh Integration Test New node injected into the live quantum optimisation as a read-only observer for 48 hours. The D-Wave annealer runs the full 2,200+ city problem including the new node but treats its outputs as advisory only. Any city whose optimal allocation changes by >3% due to the new node's presence is flagged for human review before the node goes live. Agent 4 (all active cities); Agent 7 (settlement impact); all affected city City Directors All affected city allocation changes reviewed and approved by respective City Directors before node goes active. If any change >10% → full board review. 48-hour minimum shadow period; no exceptions. All affected City Directors + CTO
N3 PQC Key Pair Generation & Distribution New node receives its unique CRYSTALS-Dilithium key pair generated on Ledger Enterprise HSM. Key distributed to the node via QKD photon-entangled channel — not via classical network. Node added to the 134/200 threshold signature quorum (threshold re-evaluated if total node count changes the quorum mathematics). Hyperledger quorum consensus; Fireblocks MPC custody for the new node; CISO key registry Key receipt confirmed on Hyperledger within 1 hour of generation. Quorum threshold re-verified: must remain ≥67% of total active nodes. If node addition pushes quorum below 67% → network halted; quorum rebalanced before new node joins. CISO + CTO
N4 Agent Scope Expansion Authorisation Each of the 7 Claude agents whose operational scope covers the new node must have their system prompts updated to include the new node's jurisdiction, language set, economic zone rules, and data access permissions. Updated prompts hashed, registered in PromptLayer, and shadow-tested against the new node's synthetic data before any live agent processing begins. All agents whose scope includes the new node's jurisdiction or operations type All affected agent prompts shadow-tested for minimum 24 hours on new node synthetic data. CAIGO approves each prompt update individually. No agent processes live data from the new node until all prompt updates are approved and hash-registered. CAIGO + CTO

What Makes a Command "Predictive"
A scheduled command fires on a clock. A predictive command fires when a signal — financial, geopolitical, environmental, cryptographic, or behavioural — crosses a defined threshold that indicates an event or threat is expected to materialise within a forward window. Delper's quantum layer continuously monitors 14 signal categories across all 2,200 city nodes, 60 jurisdictions, and 7 agent output streams. When a signal constellation matches a known precursor pattern, the corresponding predictive command is automatically staged and presented to the named authoriser for immediate execution. The authoriser can execute, delay, or dismiss — but the command is always pre-prepared and visualised on the CAIGO threat dashboard before the event arrives.

Predictive Commands — Staged Automatically, Executed on Named Authoriser Approval

Predictive Command Governance — Rules That Cannot Be Overridden

✓  Staging does not equal execution. Every predictive command is staged — fully computed and presented to the named authoriser — before any action is taken. Staging is free. Execution is governed. The authoriser always sees exactly what will happen before approving.

✓  Auto-execution is permitted only for three commands (P1, P3, P7) where delay creates a material, time-bound risk to network integrity, food security, or platform safety — and only at the partial or protective level. Auto-execution is never permitted for financial hedges (P4), regulatory policy changes (P2), covenant decisions (P6), or actual cryptographic key rotation (P5).

✓  Every auto-execution is logged, timestamped, and immediately notified to the named authoriser and CAIGO. The authoriser can reverse a P1 or P3 auto-execution within 30 minutes by issuing a reversal command. P7 (quorum protection) auto-execution cannot be reversed while the node failure risk persists.

✓  Confidence threshold governance: No predictive command is staged below 60% signal confidence. Auto-execution requires >85% confidence for P1 and >70% for P3 and P7. CAIGO reviews all staging events at the weekly W2 agent quality benchmark. Confidence threshold calibration is reviewed quarterly at Q1.

✓  Visualisation is mandatory before staging. The CAIGO threat dashboard must display the signal visualisation (from the VIZ table above) before any command is staged. A command cannot be staged for a signal the authoriser cannot see. This is enforced by the dashboard UI — the "Stage Command" button is disabled until the signal visualisation has been rendered and acknowledged.

⚡
The Answer to All Three Questions
Can all quantum scheduled commands run in parallel every second? Yes — on dedicated isolated quantum processing lanes that share zero compute resources with the business transaction layer. Every command runs continuously as a stream, not as a batch job fired on a clock.

Would business processes slow down? No — by architectural guarantee. The quantum command plane and the business transaction plane are physically partitioned on separate hardware. A quantum command consuming 100% of its allocated QPU time has zero effect on Hyperledger TPS, Claude agent latency, or payment processing.

Can errors be fixed in real time, autonomously, 24/7 without human intervention? Yes — for all operational error classes. The Autonomous Self-Healing Engine (ASHE) detects, classifies, remediates, and verifies every operational error within its defined response envelope without any human action. Humans are only invoked for irreversible financial decisions and new policy changes — never for infrastructure, agent, or quantum layer errors.

The ASHE Continuous Self-Healing Loop — Every Second, Always Running

1
COLLECT — OpenTelemetry collectors on every lane push telemetry to Dynatrace Grail lakehouse every 100ms. All 4 processing lanes, all 7 agents, all 200 nodes, all 3 regional anchors, all 7 vector stores, all Kafka topics, and all QPU utilisation metrics stream continuously into ASHE's read-only telemetry bus.
2
DETECT — Davis AI causal engine evaluates every telemetry stream against 847 defined anomaly signatures every 100ms. Not threshold-only detection: Davis AI identifies causal chains (e.g. "latency spike on node 47 is caused by Kafka consumer lag on the settlement topic, not a hardware fault") before ASHE acts — preventing wrong remediation.
3
CLASSIFY — Detected anomaly is classified against the QE-1 to QE-10 error taxonomy (above) plus 94 additional sub-classes defined in the ASHE playbook library. Classification determines: (a) which playbook to execute, (b) whether the error is within ASHE's autonomous envelope, (c) whether a human needs to be notified, and (d) priority relative to other concurrent errors. Classification completes in <20ms.
4
DECIDE — If within autonomous envelope: ASHE selects the pre-approved remediation playbook and locks in the execution plan. If outside autonomous envelope: ASHE pre-computes the human-required action, stages it on the CAIGO dashboard, and escalates to the named authoriser. In both cases, ASHE continues monitoring and running protective measures while the decision is made.
5
REMEDIATE — Playbook executes. ASHE applies the remediation action (traffic reroute, pod scale-out, model tier switch, snapshot restore, node isolation, etc.) via Kubernetes API, LangChain Router API, Kafka Admin API, Amazon AI Cloud API, or Dynatrace Automation Engine — depending on the error type. All actuator calls are logged to Hyperledger with the ASHE decision trace before execution.
6
VERIFY — ASHE waits for the telemetry signal that confirms remediation succeeded. Expected signal is defined in each playbook (e.g. "node latency below 60ms for 10 consecutive seconds"). If verification signal does not arrive within the playbook's timeout window, ASHE escalates to the next-level playbook (e.g. "replace node" instead of "rebalance traffic") and repeats from step 5.
7
LOG & LEARN — Every detection → classify → decide → remediate → verify cycle is written immutably to Hyperledger with full causal trace, playbook version, execution timestamp, and outcome. This corpus feeds the W2 weekly agent quality benchmark and the Q1 quarterly red-team analysis. ASHE playbooks are updated quarterly based on new error patterns observed. The system becomes more accurate over time.

Zero Tolerance — What This Means in Practice

✓  Zero tolerance to threats: No threat reaches the business transaction layer undetected. All 7 signal categories (S1–S7) are monitored every second. ASHE's protective measures activate before a threat peaks. The fastest threat (coordinated fraud) is met with countermeasures within 10 seconds of first signal — 48 hours before the attack wave peaks (per P1 predictive command).

✓  Zero tolerance to business process breakdown: Physical lane separation means no quantum command, no ASHE remediation action, and no scheduled task can ever consume business transaction compute. The 50,000 TPS Hyperledger SLA and the <100ms Agent 5 latency SLA are enforced by hardware reservation — they cannot be violated by any other system component.

✓  Zero human intervention for operations: All 10 QE error classes and 94 sub-classes are handled autonomously by ASHE within their defined playbooks. The platform runs, heals, and optimises itself 24/7. Humans receive informational alerts for awareness, critical alerts for oversight, and are required only for irreversible financial decisions and governance changes — none of which need to happen in the middle of the night.

✓  Error-free output guarantee: No error propagates to a business output. Every agent output is validated by the output guardrail layer before it reaches any city system, financial instrument, or resident-facing service. Errors are caught at the ASHE layer and remediated before the agent's next output cycle. If an output cannot be validated, it is withheld — never delivered in an error state.

✓  24/7 × 365 uptime target: 99.9997% (<90 seconds unplanned downtime per year across any single city node; platform-level uptime higher due to quorum redundancy across 200 nodes). This is the direct result of: 4-lane physical isolation, continuous streaming commands (no batch windows), ASHE <120ms detection-to-remediation, and warm-standby replacement nodes ready in <8 minutes.

Why Observability Is Mandatory — Not Optional
Traditional monitoring confirms that an endpoint is "up." It cannot reveal why Agent 5 (Risk & Fraud) is producing false positives at 70,000 QPS, why Agent 4's city management decisions are diverging from expected Gantt milestones, or why token costs doubled overnight. Delper's 7 Claude AI agents are non-deterministic by design: the same prompt may trigger different execution paths across city jurisdictions, producing variable costs, latencies, and outputs. At 6 billion users, 2,200 cities, and 60 sovereign jurisdictions, unobserved AI failure is a systemic risk. Observability provides causal explanations — linking telemetry across infrastructure, models, prompts, and orchestration layers — that make the invisible visible before incidents escalate into regulatory exposure, brand damage, or runaway costs.

The Core Principle — Every DPR Token Movement Is Anchored to a Real-World Event
No DPR token can leave any wallet — merchant, resident, city treasury, or investor — without a cryptographically verified, real-time transaction record and a matching invoice hash anchored on Hyperledger before the transfer is signed. This is not a policy rule. It is a smart contract constraint: the Hyperledger Besu settlement contract structurally refuses to sign any token transfer that does not carry a valid Invoice Anchor Hash (IAH) from the Delper Invoice Oracle. There is no override. There is no admin key that bypasses it. The IAH requirement is hardcoded into the contract bytecode and verified by Certora Prover. A hacker who steals a wallet private key cannot move tokens — because the stolen key alone is insufficient. The transfer also requires a live IAH that only the Delper Invoice Oracle can issue, and the oracle only issues an IAH when a verified real-world transaction exists in the supply chain, rental, settlement, or payment system.
0

Unbacked Token Transfers Possible

Structurally zero. Smart contract bytecode refuses any transfer without a valid Invoice Anchor Hash. No human can override this — it is not a permission, it is a code constraint verified by Certora Prover.

<800ms

IAH Issuance to Transfer Sign

Invoice Oracle issues the IAH within 800ms of a verified real-world transaction event. The full verify-anchor-sign cycle completes within 1.2 seconds end to end at 50,000 TPS scale.

<3s

Pullback Execution Time

When an anomalous token movement is detected post-transfer, the Autonomous Reversal Engine (ARE) executes a cryptographically enforced pullback within 3 seconds — before the token can be bridged, wrapped, or swapped.

6B

Wallets Protected

All 6 billion DPR wallets — resident, merchant, city treasury, investor, and platform — are covered by the IAH requirement. No wallet class is exempt.

1 Real-World Event Originates A verifiable economic event occurs: a merchant sale is recorded on PAX A920 Pro POS, a supply chain delivery is confirmed by Agent 6 satellite imagery, a city rental payment falls due per Agent 4 Gantt milestone, or an investor settlement is triggered by a signed FPO agreement in the SAP Ariba system. PAX POS · Agent 4 · Agent 6 · SAP Ariba · ISO 20022 payment rail T+0 (event timestamp) No event = no IAH. No IAH = transfer blocked at smart contract level. The economic event is the root of the entire chain.
2 Invoice Record Created & Hashed The event triggers automatic invoice generation in Delper's ISO 20022-compliant invoicing engine. Invoice contains: event type, counterparty wallet addresses, DPR token amount, event timestamp, jurisdiction, and supporting document reference (delivery confirmation ID, POS receipt hash, or contract clause ID). Invoice is SHA-256 hashed. Hash is the Invoice Anchor Hash (IAH). Delper Invoice Engine (ISO 20022) · SAP Ariba · CockroachDB invoice store T+0 to T+200ms No invoice = no hash. A manually constructed IAH that does not match a verifiable invoice record is rejected by the Invoice Oracle at step 3.
3 Invoice Oracle Verifies & Signs the IAH The Delper Invoice Oracle (a Chainlink-connected smart contract with off-chain adapter) verifies that: (a) the invoice exists in the invoice store, (b) the counterparty addresses match the initiating wallets, (c) the token amount is within the approved range for that event type, (d) the event timestamp is within the last 300 seconds, and (e) for any automated transfer — i.e. any transfer not carrying a dual human-authorisation signature — the token amount does not exceed 1,000 DPR tokens. If all five checks pass, the Oracle signs the IAH. If check (e) fails, the Oracle rejects the IAH request with reason code AUTO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED and logs the attempt to Hyperledger immediately. Delper Invoice Oracle · Chainlink · CockroachDB invoice store · CRYSTALS-Dilithium HSM T+200ms to T+600ms Oracle will not sign: (a) invoices older than 300 seconds (replay attack prevention), (b) amounts outside the event-type band (amount injection attack prevention), (c) wallet addresses that don't match the originating event, (d) any IAH that has already been used in a prior transfer (single-use enforcement), (e) any automated transfer exceeding 1,000 DPR tokens — AUTO_LIMIT_EXCEEDED rejection, logged immediately to Hyperledger and Agent 5 alerted.
4 Smart Contract Validates IAH Before Signing Transfer The Hyperledger Besu DPR settlement contract receives the transfer request alongside the Oracle-signed IAH. Before signing the transfer: it verifies the Oracle's CRYSTALS-Dilithium signature on the IAH, checks the IAH has not been used before (nullifier registry), confirms the token amount in the transfer matches the IAH exactly (no rounding or truncation exploits), confirms the destination wallet is not on the OFAC/FATF block list, and enforces the 1,000 DPR automated transfer cap as a second independent check — the contract reads the transfer's automation flag directly from the transaction metadata and rejects any automated transfer above 1,000 DPR tokens regardless of what the Oracle signed. This dual-enforcement means the cap cannot be bypassed even if the Oracle is compromised. Only if all checks pass does the contract sign the transfer and emit the DPR transfer event. Hyperledger Besu settlement contract · CRYSTALS-Dilithium verifier · Nullifier registry · Agent 1 block list · Auto-cap enforcement module (Certora-verified bytecode) T+600ms to T+800ms Any single check failure: transfer reverted. Reversion is recorded on Hyperledger with reason code. Agent 5 (Fraud) alerted if same wallet triggers 3 reverted transfers within 60 seconds.
5 IAH Nullified — One-Time Use Enforced Once a transfer is signed and emitted, the IAH is immediately written to the on-chain nullifier registry and marked as consumed. It can never be reused. The nullifier registry is append-only on Hyperledger — entries cannot be deleted. A replay attack using a previously valid IAH will be rejected at step 4 the instant the consumed nullifier is found. Hyperledger nullifier registry (append-only) · Agent 5 nullifier monitoring T+800ms (concurrent with transfer emission) Without nullifier: a hacker who captures a valid IAH could replay it against the same wallet repeatedly. Nullifier makes this structurally impossible — each IAH is a one-time cryptographic voucher.
6 Full Audit Record Published to Hyperledger The complete chain — event record → invoice hash → Oracle signature → contract validation → transfer emission → nullifier — is written as a single atomic log entry to Hyperledger within 1.2 seconds of the original economic event. Every DPR token transfer ever made has a complete, immutable, publicly auditable chain of custody from real-world event to on-chain settlement. SBLC banks, regulators, and auditors can verify any transfer's legitimacy by inspecting this chain. Hyperledger audit log · Merkle root publication (6-hourly) · Agent 1 (AML review of full chain) T+800ms to T+1,200ms Without this record, SBLC banks cannot verify token integrity as covenant collateral. This audit chain is the legal proof of legitimate token movement for all 60 jurisdictions.

The Rule — Hardcoded, Not Configurable
No automated system — including all 7 Claude AI agents, ASHE, the Invoice Oracle, any API integration, any scheduled quantum command, any third-party payment processor, and any PAX POS terminal operating in auto-settlement mode — may transfer more than 1,000 DPR tokens in a single transaction without dual human authorisation. This is not a soft limit enforced by policy. It is a three-layer hard enforcement: (1) Invoice Oracle rejects the IAH issuance, (2) Hyperledger Besu settlement contract reverts the transfer, and (3) Agent 5 Kafka monitor intercepts and holds any transfer that slips past the first two. All three layers must fail simultaneously for an automated transfer >1,000 DPR to succeed — which is structurally impossible under normal operation and requires coordinated compromise of Oracle + contract + Kafka monitor simultaneously, which itself triggers the F2 Layer 4 adversarial hardening response.

1,000 DPR Token Automated Transfer Cap — Three-Layer Enforcement · No Single Override

Micro-Batching (same destination) Agent 5 aggregates all automated transfers to the same destination wallet in any rolling 10-minute window. If the aggregate exceeds 5,000 DPR across more than 5 transactions — regardless of each individual transaction being below 1,000 DPR — the pattern is flagged as a split transaction attack. ARE freezes both source and destination wallets. All in-flight Kafka transfers to the same destination are intercepted and held in PendingReview. CISO + CCO review within 30 minutes. If split-attack confirmed: all transfers in the batch reversed; wallets permanently flagged. <5 seconds from 6th transaction to wallet freeze
Fan-Out (same source, many destinations) Agent 5 monitors any source wallet sending automated transfers to more than 10 distinct destination wallets within any rolling 60-minute window where the aggregate exceeds 10,000 DPR. Fan-out is consistent with a hacked wallet distributing tokens across mule wallets. Source wallet frozen immediately. All destination wallets placed in PendingReview — tokens held pending CISO review. Transfers to wallets with no prior relationship with the source wallet are reversed autonomously; known counterparties released after CISO review. <10 seconds from 11th destination wallet to source freeze
Time-Delayed Batching (same destination, hours apart) Agent 5 maintains a 24-hour rolling aggregate per wallet pair. If any source-destination pair accumulates >50,000 DPR in automated transfers within 24 hours without a corresponding DHAO on file, the pattern is flagged. Quantum D2 Grover index includes time-delayed batching as a named fraud pattern updated daily. Source wallet flagged for manual review. Next automated transfer to same destination intercepted pending CISO review. Confirmed transfers not reversed (finality applies) but source wallet requires DHAO for all future transfers to that destination until 24-hour window clears. <1 second detection (D2 continuous stream); next transfer intercepted before confirmation
Oracle Flooding (rapid <1,000 DPR IAH requests) Invoice Oracle rate-limiter: maximum 10 automated IAH issuances per wallet per minute. Any wallet requesting more than 10 automated IAHs in 60 seconds triggers rate throttling. More than 5 IAHs per minute to the same destination triggers an immediate split-attack flag to Agent 5. Oracle suspends IAH issuance for the flagging wallet for 10 minutes. Agent 5 reviews the pattern. If split-attack confirmed: permanent Oracle blacklist for that wallet; CISO notified; all recent transfers re-examined via ARE. <60 seconds from rate-limit trigger to IAH suspension
↗

Split Transaction Attack Prevention — Stopping Hackers Who Split Large Transfers Into <1,000 DPR Batches

1,000 DPR Cap — Why This Number, What It Covers, What It Doesn't

✓  Why 1,000 DPR: At Year 4 token price of $107.17/DPR, 1,000 DPR ≈ $107,170 USD. This is a meaningful transaction size for merchants and residents, but below the threshold where automated disbursement without human oversight poses systemic risk. The cap is in DPR tokens, not USD — so as the token appreciates, the cap becomes more conservative in dollar terms over time, providing increasing protection through the 21-year programme.

✓  What "automated" means: Any transfer initiated by software — all 7 Claude AI agents, ASHE, scheduled quantum commands, API integrations, PAX POS auto-settlement, merchant batch processing, and third-party processors. A transfer is only non-automated if it carries the CRYSTALS-Dilithium signatures of the required number of named human approvers (DHAO) embedded in the transaction metadata.

✓  Three independent enforcement layers: Oracle bytecode (Certora-verified) + Hyperledger settlement contract auto-cap module (Certora-verified) + Agent 5 Kafka monitor. All three must fail simultaneously for an automated >1,000 DPR transfer to succeed. Each bypass attempt is logged independently to Hyperledger.

✓  Split transaction protection: Micro-batching, fan-out, time-delayed batching, and Oracle flooding detectors close all known circumvention vectors. A hacker cannot send 50 transactions of 999 DPR to bypass the cap — the aggregate detectors catch this pattern and freeze the wallets before the total exceeds 5,000 DPR.

✓  DHAO cannot be waived by any single person: Not GK Bharta, not the CFO, not the Chairman. The DHAO requires the minimum number of signatures for the applicable tier — a single powerful actor cannot unilaterally authorise a large automated disbursement. This protects against both external hackers and insider threat at the highest level of the organisation.

⚠️
When Pullback Is Triggered
The IAH system prevents unbacked transfers. But some attack vectors attempt to corrupt the underlying invoice — not bypass the IAH check. A supply chain fraud that generates a fake delivery confirmation, a merchant collusion attack that inflates a POS receipt, or a compromised Oracle that signs a fraudulent IAH can all result in a transfer that passed the IAH check but was backed by a fraudulent invoice. The Autonomous Reversal Engine (ARE) operates as a second layer of defence: it monitors every completed transfer for post-transfer anomaly signals and executes a cryptographic pullback within 3 seconds if a fraudulent backing event is detected — before the tokens can leave the Delper ecosystem.
TR-1 · Invoice Source Fraud Agent 5 cross-references the invoice's supporting document ID against the originating system (PAX receipt database, SAP Ariba contract log, Agent 4 milestone database). If the document ID does not exist in the source system — i.e. the invoice was constructed against a fabricated document — Agent 5 flags the transfer within 2 seconds of the Hyperledger emission event. ARE issues a CRYSTALS-Dilithium-signed PullbackOrder transaction to the settlement contract. The contract freezes the destination wallet immediately (no tokens can leave) and initiates a reverse transfer of the exact token amount to the originating wallet. Frozen wallet state logged to Hyperledger with ARE decision trace. <3 seconds from Agent 5 flag to frozen destination CISO + Agent 1 review within 1 hour. If fraud confirmed: reverse transfer executed and wallet permanently frozen. If false positive: ARE reversal reversed by CISO command; frozen state lifted. Freeze: autonomous. Permanent reversal: CISO-authorised.
TR-2 · Oracle Compromise Signal Agent 5 detects that the Invoice Oracle issued more than 3 IAHs per second for the same wallet — a pattern consistent with a compromised Oracle signing in bulk. Alternatively, the Oracle's CRYSTALS-Dilithium signing key shows a rotation timestamp mismatch against the D3 key rotation log — indicating the key was rotated outside the scheduled process. ARE immediately suspends the compromised Oracle instance and activates the backup Oracle (hot standby, separate HSM, separate Amazon AI Cloud region). All transfers signed by the compromised Oracle in the prior 300 seconds are placed in a Disputed state on Hyperledger — not reversed, but frozen pending ARE review. ARE re-verifies each disputed transfer against the source invoice. Clean transfers: Disputed → Confirmed. Fraudulent transfers: Disputed → Reversed. <1 second to Oracle suspension; backup Oracle live within 5 seconds; review of disputed transfers complete within 90 seconds CISO + CTO notified immediately. CTO authorises permanent decommission of compromised Oracle. CAIGO reviews all confirmed/reversed decisions within 24 hours. Oracle suspension: autonomous. Final reversal decisions: ARE with CISO review.
TR-3 · Velocity Anomaly (Wallet Draining) Any wallet — regardless of balance — that executes more than 5 outbound transfers totalling >10× its 30-day average daily volume within any 10-minute window is flagged by Agent 5 as a potential draining attack. This covers both hacked wallets and insider theft patterns. ARE freezes the wallet immediately (no further outbound transfers). Existing in-flight transfers in the Kafka settlement queue are intercepted and held in a PendingReview state before Hyperledger confirmation. Held transfers are individually reviewed by ARE against the IAH chain: if each held transfer has a valid IAH and a verifiable source invoice, it is released. If any held transfer lacks a complete valid chain, it is reversed. <2 seconds to wallet freeze; in-flight transfer interception within Kafka settlement window (<500ms before Hyperledger confirmation) CISO notified immediately. Wallet owner notified via city management system. Wallet unfrozen only by CISO command after ARE review confirms clean transfers. Disputed transfers require CCO + CISO joint authorisation to finalise reversal. Freeze and interception: autonomous. Unfreeze: CISO-authorised.
TR-4 · Cross-Chain Bridge Attempt DPR tokens are Hyperledger-native and are not designed to be bridged to external chains (Ethereum mainnet, Solana, etc.). Any transfer to a wallet address that matches the signature pattern of a cross-chain bridge contract — detected by Agent 5's bridge address registry — is flagged as a potential theft exfiltration attempt. ARE immediately intercepts the transfer in the Kafka settlement queue before Hyperledger confirmation. The transfer is suspended in PendingReview. Agent 1 (AML) reviews the bridge destination address against FATF and Chainalysis Reactor blacklists. If the bridge is to a sanctioned or high-risk address: ARE reverses the transfer autonomously. If the bridge is to a legitimate institutional custodian (Fireblocks, Ledger Enterprise): transfer released with additional audit log entry noting the cross-chain flag. <500ms interception in Kafka queue; Agent 1 review complete <30 seconds; release or reversal within 45 seconds Agent 1 autonomous review for high-risk addresses. CCO notified for any bridge to non-sanctioned address. All bridge-attempt flags logged to Hyperledger and included in monthly M4 bias and W4 compliance reports. Interception: autonomous. Release for clean bridges: Agent 1 autonomous. Reversal for sanctioned bridges: autonomous.
TR-5 · Nullifier Replay Attack An attacker attempts to reuse a previously consumed IAH — either by replaying a captured network packet or by constructing a transfer request with a stolen IAH before the nullifier was written. Agent 5 monitors the nullifier registry in real time; any transfer request containing an IAH that is already in the nullifier registry is flagged immediately. ARE rejects the transfer at the smart contract level (step 4 of the IAH system — nullifier check fails). No tokens move. The attempting wallet is immediately flagged in the OFAC-equivalent Delper block list. If 3 replay attempts originate from the same wallet within 60 seconds: wallet is frozen autonomously by ARE, and Agent 5 triggers the P1 predictive command (coordinated fraud precursor) at 100% confidence — bypassing the normal 85% confidence threshold. <100ms (nullifier check is in-block-proposal; no tokens move) CISO notified on first replay attempt. Wallet freeze (after 3 attempts) is autonomous. P1 predictive command requires CISO acknowledgement but countermeasures already running. Transfer rejection and nullifier check: fully autonomous and instantaneous. Wallet freeze after 3 attempts: autonomous.

Cap enforcement: fully autonomous at both Oracle and contract. Wallet freeze after 3 attempts: autonomous. DHAO override: requires dual human sign-off — cannot be waived by any single person including GK Bharta.

Settlement Requires Breach-Clear — Not Just Time
The previous model granted finality after a passive 90-second window with no anomaly flag. That model is replaced. Every DPR token transfer — merchant, rental, SBLC, or treasury — now requires an active Settlement Breach Clearance (SBC) signal from Agent 5 and ASHE before the Hyperledger settlement contract will mark it as final. The SBC signal is not a timer. It is a cryptographically signed confirmation that the transfer, the originating wallet, the IAH, the Invoice Oracle, and the destination wallet have each passed a real-time breach-status check and are confirmed clean. Only when the SBC signal is issued does the settlement contract emit the TransferFinalized event. Without SBC, the transfer remains in PendingSettlement state — it is recorded on Hyperledger but not final, and ACRE can still reverse it. A transfer in PendingSettlement is visible to the recipient but explicitly marked as uncleared on all Delper interfaces.

SBC

SBC Pipeline — How the Breach-Clear Signal Is Generated and Verified

SBC — What Changes From the Previous 90-Second Model

✓  Active gate, not passive timer: Previously, finality required only that 90 seconds passed with no anomaly flag. Now, finality requires a positive SBC signal — 5 active checks that must each pass. Absence of a flag is not sufficient. A positive confirmation of clean status is required.

✓  Settlement state is visible: Every transfer is in one of three states — PendingSettlement (SBC not yet issued), TransferFinalized (SBC issued, settlement complete), or Reversed (pullback executed). Merchants, residents, and investors can see this state in real time on their Delper wallet interface. No transfer appears as "complete" until SBC is issued.

✓  SBC re-attempted automatically every 5 seconds: A transfer in PendingSettlement is not abandoned. The SBC pipeline retries every 5 seconds until all checks pass or the transfer is escalated. Most legitimate transfers clear within 2 seconds — the retry mechanism handles edge cases where a momentary breach alert clears before the next SBC attempt.

✓  SBC Oracle is independent of the Invoice Oracle: A compromised Invoice Oracle (TR-2, BC-2) cannot generate a false SBC signal. The SBC Oracle uses a separately maintained CRYSTALS-Dilithium key, a separate HSM partition, and a separate Amazon AI Cloud region from the Invoice Oracle. Compromising both simultaneously requires breaching two independently governed cryptographic systems — which itself triggers BC-1 and ACRE.

✓  Zero settlement during active breach: If any BC-1 to BC-6 breach class is active anywhere on the platform, SBC-1 and SBC-2 will withhold settlement for any transfer involving an affected wallet. Unaffected wallets continue settling normally — SBC checks are per-transfer, not platform-wide pauses. The platform does not freeze during a breach; it surgically holds only the affected transfers.

D2 · Fraud Pattern Index (Daily Stream) Grover amplitude search continuously updates the IAH fraud pattern library. New attack vectors discovered in TR-1 to TR-6 events are ingested into the fraud index within the same day's D2 stream, so the next occurrence of the same attack pattern is caught at the IAH check stage (step 3) rather than post-transfer. The system learns from every attack attempt. Continuous 1-second stream; snapshot published daily 01:00 UTC
QE-10 · Merkle Root Mismatch (ASHE) If a hacker compromises a validator node and attempts to rewrite a completed token transfer in the ledger (changing the destination wallet in a confirmed block), the continuous Merkle root verification (D4) detects the mismatch within one block proposal window (<1 second). ASHE isolates the node immediately per QE-10. The corrupted block is never accepted into the canonical chain — the transfer history is immutable. Per-block continuous at 50,000 TPS; full daily tree audit at 00:00 UTC
W1 · Cross-City Settlement Reconciliation (Weekly) All inter-city DPR token flows for the week are reconciled against the IAH audit chain. Any settlement gap — a token movement recorded on-chain without a matching IAH audit entry — is flagged as a potential ledger integrity violation. No gap has ever been expected to exist if the IAH system is functioning correctly; any gap is therefore a system error or attack signal, not a normal variance. Every Monday 02:00 UTC; CFO + CAIGO sign-off
M2 · PQC Key Integrity Audit (Monthly) The Invoice Oracle's CRYSTALS-Dilithium signing key is included in the monthly PQC key integrity audit. Any key that has exceeded its rotation age, shows signs of reuse, or has a duplicate detected is flagged immediately — preventing the Oracle Compromise (TR-2) attack vector from persisting undetected between quarterly red-team cycles. 1st of each month; CISO + CTO joint sign-off
Q1 · Red-Team Quantum Simulation (Quarterly) The adversarial D-Wave instance specifically attempts to break the IAH system: constructing fake invoice hashes, replaying nullified IAHs, exploiting Oracle key material, and attempting amount injection attacks at quantum speed. Every quarter, the red-team simulation tests whether new quantum capabilities have opened any new attack vector against the token pullback architecture. Results drive ARE playbook updates. Jan / Apr / Jul / Oct; CTO + CISO + GK Bharta review
P1 · Predictive Command — Coordinated Fraud (F1c) When Agent 5 detects the S1 coordinated fraud precursor (10,000+ new wallet activations with similar origination patterns), it now also pre-loads the ARE with a heightened pullback sensitivity profile: TR-1 through TR-5 thresholds are all tightened by 50% for the flagged wallet cluster. The ARE is already in high-alert mode before the attack wave peaks — it does not wait for the first fraudulent transfer to occur. Event-triggered; 48–72 hours before projected attack peak

Integration with ASHE & Quantum Command Schedule — Continuous Token Integrity 24/7

Token Pullback — Governance & Regulatory Summary

✓  Structural prevention: The IAH requirement is hardcoded in smart contract bytecode verified by Certora Prover. No admin key, no governance vote, and no human action can bypass it. A stolen private key alone is insufficient to move tokens — the attacker also needs a live Oracle-signed IAH, which requires a real economic event.

✓  Autonomous reversal within 3 seconds: ARE executes pullback for TR-1 through TR-7 attack classes autonomously, within 3 seconds of detection, before tokens can be bridged, swapped, or exfiltrated. Freezes are reversible by CISO. Permanent reversals require CISO + CCO joint authorisation.

✓  Confirmed breach triggers total pullback (F6a): When a breach is confirmed — not just suspected — the Cascade Reversal Engine (ACRE) executes a network-wide sweep of all tainted tokens across all hops with no depth limit, within 10 seconds. See Section F6a for the full breach class definitions, ACRE execution mechanics, and Recovery Vault disposition process.

✓  Settlement only after breach-clear confirmed (SBC Gate): No transfer becomes final without a positive Settlement Breach Clearance (SBC) signal from Agent 5 and ASHE — 5 active checks covering source wallet, destination wallet, IAH integrity, network integrity, and agent/system integrity, all run in parallel and completed within 2 seconds. A passive timer is no longer sufficient for finality. Every transfer remains in PendingSettlement until the SBC Oracle issues a CRYSTALS-Dilithium-signed BreachClearSignal. See the SBC pipeline table within this section for full check details.

✓  FATF Recommendation 16 (Travel Rule): The IAH audit chain — event → invoice → Oracle signature → transfer → nullifier — constitutes Delper's Travel Rule compliance record for all DPR token transfers above the FATF threshold. Agent 1 (AML) reviews the IAH chain for every high-value transfer. No transfer above threshold is confirmed without an IAH that satisfies Travel Rule originator and beneficiary information requirements.

✓  EU Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) Article 83: Asset-referenced token issuers must maintain adequate reserves and prevent unauthorised token issuance. The IAH system's structural zero-unbacked-transfer guarantee, combined with the monthly M3 token floor recomputation and the Certora-verified smart contract, constitutes Delper's MiCA Article 83 compliance architecture for DPR token integrity.

✓  SBLC Bank Covenant: All Tier 1 anchor banks require that DPR tokens used as pledge collateral maintain an unbroken IAH audit chain for every transfer in their history. The Hyperledger audit log provides this chain, immutably, for every token in the pledge pool. Banks can verify token legitimacy for any specific token by inspecting its complete IAH chain from the Hyperledger explorer.

🚨
When a Breach Is Confirmed — Every Token Touched by That Breach Is Recalled
The F6 pullback mechanisms (TR-1 to TR-7) handle individual suspicious transfers. F6a handles something different: a confirmed breach — where Agent 5, ASHE, or the quantum Merkle verification has established that a wallet, wallet cluster, Oracle instance, or ledger segment has been definitively compromised. At that point, the response is not surgical. It is total. Every DPR token that moved through or currently sits in any wallet connected to the breach is pulled back autonomously by the Cascade Reversal Engine (ACRE) — a dedicated Hyperledger smart contract function that executes a network-wide atomic sweep, traces the full transaction graph of the breach, and reverses every tainted transfer in reverse chronological order until the ledger is returned to its pre-breach state. ACRE operates without human intervention for the sweep execution. Human authority governs what happens to the recovered tokens after the sweep completes.
<10s

Network-Wide Sweep Time

ACRE executes a quantum-accelerated transaction graph traversal across all 6B wallets and 200 nodes, identifies every tainted wallet, and issues simultaneous PullbackOrder transactions to all of them within 10 seconds of a confirmed breach classification.

∞

Hops Traced

ACRE follows the token trail with no depth limit. If a stolen token was transferred 20 wallets deep before the breach was detected, ACRE traces all 20 hops and issues pullback to every wallet in the chain simultaneously.

100%

Tainted Token Coverage

Every token that passed through a compromised wallet — not just the originally stolen amount — is recalled. Partial recovery is not acceptable. The ledger is restored to its exact pre-breach state or ACRE holds all tainted wallets frozen until resolution is complete.

7yr

Audit Chain Retained

Every ACRE sweep is written as an immutable atomic record on Hyperledger. The breach, the traversal graph, every pullback issued, and every recovery confirmed is retained in full for 7 years — FATF, MiCA, and EU AI Act compliant.

Breach Classes That Trigger Total Pullback — Confirmed Threshold Required Before ACRE Activates

F6a

Breach-Triggered Total Token Pullback — All Tokens From All Affected Wallets Recalled on Confirmed Breach

Security · Total Pullback
1
BREACH CLASSIFICATION RECEIVED — ACRE receives a confirmed breach classification from Agent 5 or ASHE with: breach class (BC-1 to BC-6), origin wallet(s) or block range, breach timestamp, and the pre-computed transaction graph from the D2 Grover index. ACRE does not re-investigate — it acts on the classification immediately. Time: T+0.
2
QUANTUM GRAPH TRAVERSAL — ACRE submits the origin wallet(s) to the D-Wave quantum annealer for a full transaction graph expansion. The annealer traces every outbound transfer from every tainted wallet, then every outbound transfer from those recipients, recursively, with no depth limit. The output is a complete set of tainted wallets ranked by: (a) tokens currently held from the breach, (b) hops from origin, (c) time since last activity. Graph expansion completes in <2 seconds for up to 10,000 wallet hops. Time: T+2s.
3
SIMULTANEOUS FREEZE — ALL TAINTED WALLETS — ACRE issues a NetworkFreeze transaction to the Hyperledger settlement contract listing all tainted wallets from the graph traversal. The contract freezes all listed wallets simultaneously in a single atomic transaction — no wallet in the list can execute any outbound transfer from this point forward. Freeze is recorded on Hyperledger with the ACRE breach classification as the authorisation record. Time: T+3s.
4
TAINTED AMOUNT CALCULATION PER WALLET — For each frozen wallet, ACRE calculates the exact tainted token amount: the number of DPR tokens in that wallet that can be traced back to the breach origin via the transaction graph. Wallets may hold both tainted and legitimate tokens. ACRE calculates only the tainted portion — legitimate holdings are not frozen beyond what is needed for the pullback. Time: T+4s (quantum-accelerated parallel calculation across all wallets simultaneously).
5
REVERSE CHRONOLOGICAL PULLBACK EXECUTION — ACRE issues PullbackOrder transactions in reverse chronological order: the most recent tainted transfers are recalled first (these have the least finality and are most recoverable), working back to the origin. Each PullbackOrder transfers the calculated tainted amount from the destination wallet back to a dedicated ACRE Recovery Vault — a Hyperledger escrow address controlled jointly by CISO + CFO multi-sig. Tokens accumulate in the Recovery Vault until the sweep is complete. Time: T+5s to T+10s depending on graph size.
6
SWEEP COMPLETION VERIFICATION — ACRE verifies that the total tokens recovered into the Recovery Vault match the total tainted amount calculated in step 4. If the totals match: sweep confirmed complete, all frozen wallets unfrozen (except the origin breach wallet), and the Recovery Vault balance is reported to CISO + CFO. If the totals do not match (tokens moved between graph expansion and freeze): ACRE re-runs the graph traversal from the frozen state and issues supplementary pullbacks for any remaining tainted amounts. Time: T+10s to T+15s for verification.
7
RECOVERY VAULT DISPOSITION — Tokens in the Recovery Vault are held in multi-sig escrow (CISO + CFO) until post-breach review is complete. Legitimate recipients who received tokens from the breach unknowingly (e.g. a merchant who accepted a payment later found to originate from a hacked wallet) are identified during CISO review. Their tokens are restored from the Delper platform reserve — Delper absorbs the loss, not the innocent recipient. The breach-origin tokens remain in the Recovery Vault for legal proceedings. Time: CISO + CFO review within 24 hours of sweep completion.
Tokens already converted to ETH or fiat via DEX Once a DPR token is swapped for ETH on an external DEX, the DPR token is burned on the Hyperledger side and the ETH exists on a separate chain under a separate address. ACRE cannot reach across chain boundaries — this is by design (preventing ACRE from affecting non-Delper assets). Chainalysis Reactor traces the ETH address. Legal freeze request issued to the DEX operator (if centralised) or flagged to Interpol/FBI for on-chain forensics (if decentralised). TR-4 cross-chain bridge interception (F6) catches most conversions before they complete — ACRE is the fallback for any that slipped through. Delper restores the equivalent DPR amount to the affected wallet from the platform reserve. Legal recovery proceedings seek restitution from the attacker. No innocent party bears the loss.
Tokens in a finalised merchant settlement (>90 seconds confirmed) The F6 finality rule protects confirmed merchant settlements after the 90-second ARE review window. ACRE respects this finality — reversing confirmed merchant payments would destroy platform trust and violate ISO 20022 payment finality. The merchant's settlement is protected. The tainted amount is absorbed by Delper's platform reserve — Delper is the loss-bearer, not the merchant. If the merchant was a knowing participant in the breach, this is a separate criminal matter handled by Agent 1 and CCO. Delper bears the loss for confirmed merchant settlements paid from breach-origin tokens. This is covered by the $80M/yr bug bounty and legal recovery budget (F3 Tier 2 + Tier 3).
Tokens in a confirmed SBLC drawdown payment SBLC drawdowns require CFO + Chairman dual authorisation and are governed by international banking law (UCP 600). ACRE cannot reverse a payment that an SBLC bank has already accepted — this would constitute a documentary credit breach. SBLC bank notified immediately via the F4 Class A financial misaction protocol. Legal counsel engaged in the bank's jurisdiction. If the drawdown was triggered by a BC-2 Oracle compromise: Certora formal verification report provided to the bank as evidence that the triggering instruction was fraudulent. Repayment negotiated under the applicable governing law. CFO + GK Bharta lead the bank negotiation. Delper's $5T ESG bond programme and $47.16T/yr rental income provide ample balance sheet to absorb any drawdown reversal obligation. This scenario is assessed as extremely low probability given the CFO + Chairman dual-auth requirement for all SBLC drawdowns.
Tokens sent to a wallet in a jurisdiction that has legally seized them If a regulator or law enforcement agency in any of the 60 jurisdictions has legally seized tokens in a wallet (e.g. under a court freezing order), ACRE's PullbackOrder will be blocked by the legal hold flag on that wallet — which takes precedence over ACRE in the contract logic. Legal counsel in the relevant jurisdiction engaged immediately. Hyperledger audit log and ACRE sweep report provided to the seizing authority as evidence of the breach and legitimate ownership claim. Recovery timeline subject to the local legal process. CCO + General Counsel lead the legal recovery. Timeline is jurisdiction-dependent. Delper retains the claim on the seized tokens via the full IAH audit chain proving their pre-breach ownership.
