Tokens ACRE Cannot Pull Back — And What Happens Instead

ACRE

ACRE Execution — How the Cascade Reversal Works in Practice

Breach-Triggered Total Pullback — Governance Summary

✓  Total sweep, not partial: On confirmed breach, ACRE recalls every tainted token across every hop with no depth limit. There is no partial recovery — either the full tainted amount is returned to the Recovery Vault, or ACRE continues until it is. The ledger is restored to its pre-breach state or all tainted wallets remain frozen.

✓  <10 seconds from confirmed breach to network-wide freeze: Quantum graph traversal (2s) + simultaneous network freeze (3s) + tainted amount calculation (4s) + first pullback orders (10s). Business wallets not connected to the breach are unaffected throughout — ACRE operates on the dedicated self-healing lane with no interference to the business transaction lane.

✓  Innocent recipients are protected: Legitimate merchants, residents, and investors who received tokens that originated in a breach are made whole from the Delper platform reserve. They do not bear the loss. The Recovery Vault disposition process (step 7) ensures this within 24 hours of sweep completion.

✓  ACRE cannot be used as a weapon: ACRE requires a confirmed breach classification from Agent 5 or ASHE — it cannot be triggered by a human command alone. This prevents ACRE from being used by a rogue insider to freeze arbitrary wallets. The only way to activate ACRE is through the defined BC-1 to BC-6 breach classification pipeline, which itself is governed by the ASHE autonomous envelope and the F1a quantum processing boundary.

✓  Every ACRE execution is a permanent Hyperledger record: Breach classification → graph traversal → network freeze → tainted calculations → pullback orders → verification → Recovery Vault transfer — all seven steps written as a single atomic audit block to Hyperledger, timestamped, retained 7 years. Regulators, SBLC banks, and auditors have full visibility into every ACRE sweep ever executed.

✓  FATF, MiCA, and EU AI Act alignment: Each confirmed breach that triggers ACRE requires a FATF SAR from Agent 1 within 24 hours (BC-4 and BC-6), a MiCA Article 83 incident report within 72 hours (BC-2 Oracle compromise), and an EU AI Act Article 9 risk management documentation update from CAIGO within 7 days of any BC-5 rogue agent breach. The ACRE sweep record constitutes the primary evidence document for all three filings.

Policy Purpose & Authority
This policy exists to shape the behaviour of every person and system that interacts with or is affected by Delper's 7 Claude AI agents — not to satisfy auditors. It is readable in under 15 minutes. It covers what AI may do, what it may not do, and where human judgment is required before AI output can be acted upon. Authority: Chief AI Governance Officer (CAIGO), reporting to GK Bharta (Chairman). This policy supersedes any departmental AI usage assumption not covered herein. Effective Year 4 (IPO). Reviewed at every FPO tranche and annually thereafter (see Milestone Table governance cadence column).

✅ WHERE AI IS PERMITTED

Agent 1: SAR pre-drafting, real-time AML screening, Chainalysis forensics tagging — subject to CCO review before filing.

Agent 2: Regulatory feed summarisation, jurisdiction alerts, policy comparison — read-only intelligence only.

Agent 3: KYC document verification, merchant risk scoring, onboarding automation up to standard-risk tier.

Agent 4: Construction milestone tracking, procurement recommendation, satellite imagery analysis, Gantt generation — below $500M disbursement threshold.

Agent 5: Real-time transaction monitoring at 70K QPS, fraud pattern flagging, wallet freeze recommendation below $10M.

Agent 6: Crop yield modelling, farm-to-city logistics scheduling, agronomy recommendations — within Farm Data Tier 3 only.

Agent 7: ETH pool monitoring, inflow reporting, gold purchase scheduling recommendation below $500M — recommendations only, no autonomous execution.

🚫 WHERE AI IS PROHIBITED

No Claude agent may autonomously execute any financially irreversible, legally binding, or operationally irreversible action without named human confirmation.

Prohibited autonomous actions: SBLC drawdown initiation · gold vault transfer execution · DPR token pledge draw · permanent wallet ban · city permit execution · land title record modification · SAR submission to regulator · ESG bond covenant breach notification · FPO pricing decision · cross-border data transfer not covered by active MLAT.

Prohibited data access: No agent may access data outside its defined Tier without CAIGO written approval. No agent output may be shared with third parties (including SBLC banks) without CCO and General Counsel sign-off.

AI-generated summaries of personal resident data may not be the sole basis for any decision affecting a resident's access to city services.

👤 WHERE HUMAN JUDGMENT IS REQUIRED

Any single transaction >$1B — Agent 7: CFO + Chairman dual authorisation.

Wallet freeze >$10M — Agent 5: CISO + CCO.

SAR filing in any jurisdiction — Agent 1: CCO confirmation within 4 hours.

City approval advancement — Agent 4: City Director + CTO dual approval.

High-risk jurisdiction merchant onboarding — Agent 3: Senior Compliance Officer.

Food sovereignty volume intervention — Agent 6: Regional Agronomy Director.

Any AI output influencing a formal record (city permit, SBLC milestone, regulatory submission, financial statement) must be human-verified, timestamped, and attributed. The AI output is the draft. The human decision is the record.

When AI output is wrong and acted upon: accountability rests with the named approver, not the agent. This policy transfers strategic risk from the platform administrator to the executive layer where it belongs.

01What data classes are prohibited from AI systems?Confidential legal opinions · pending litigation files · cross-border personal data not covered by active MLAT · agent-to-agent data sharing outside defined tiers · classified SBLC negotiation materials. Each agent's Tier definition (Agent Permission Matrix in Section C3) constitutes the data access boundary.
02When must AI outputs be human-verified before acting?All financially irreversible actions above defined thresholds · all regulatory submissions · all formal records (permits, SBLC milestones, financial statements) · all decisions affecting individual residents' access to city services. See the "Irreversible Actions Require" and "Human-in-the-Loop Trigger" columns in the Agent Permission Matrix.
03Who owns the decision if AI output is wrong?The named human approver who signed off on the action. If no human approved it, accountability defaults to the CAIGO and the domain executive (CCO for Agents 1–2; CTO for Agent 4; CISO for Agent 5; CFO for Agent 7). Platform administrators are never accountability holders for AI output correctness — this policy explicitly lifts that burden.
04Are AI interactions logged under existing audit policies?Yes. Every agent action is logged immutably on Hyperledger with timestamp, input prompt hash, output hash, and named approver. These logs are subject to the same retention and audit requirements as human-authored financial records — minimum 7 years, or as required by the most restrictive applicable jurisdiction. Retrievable within 30 minutes of request.
05Does AI operate within existing permission models?Yes, and more specifically: each agent's Tier is defined in the Agent Permission Matrix and enforced at API and Hyperledger node level — not just as a policy statement. Tier definitions are narrower than platform-level access permissions by design. Tier 3 agents (Agent 6) cannot access Tier 1 data regardless of platform permissions. This prevents the "discoverability gap" — where content technically accessible becomes AI-surfaceable at scale beyond what the permission model intended.

Why Bias Testing Is a Legal and Ethical Obligation
EU AI Act Article 10 requires that training, validation, and testing datasets for high-risk AI systems be free from discriminatory patterns. OECD AI Principle 1.3 requires AI that does not discriminate on protected grounds. At Delper's scale — automated decisions affecting food access, financial services, and housing for 6 billion people across 60 jurisdictions — undetected bias is a systemic risk of the highest order. Agents 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 all make or inform decisions that can advantage or disadvantage individuals based on characteristics that must be protected under international human rights law. This section defines mandatory bias testing protocols that must be completed before any agent goes live in a production environment.

Provider vs Deployer — Distinct Obligations Under EU AI Act
Delper uses Anthropic's Claude models as the AI provider. Delper is the deployer of those models in a high-risk context. Under EU AI Act Articles 25–26, the deployer (Delper) carries specific obligations that are separate from and additional to the provider's (Anthropic's) obligations. Deployers of high-risk AI systems must: (a) implement appropriate human oversight; (b) assign a competent natural person for oversight tasks; (c) ensure the system is used in accordance with the provider's instructions of use; (d) monitor operations and report serious incidents; and (e) maintain logs for at least 6 months. These obligations are Delper's — not Anthropic's — and cannot be contracted away to Anthropic.

Why Explainability Is a Legal Right, Not a Design Option
GDPR Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions that significantly affect them — and the right to obtain a meaningful explanation of the logic involved when such decisions are made. EU AI Act Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be transparent enough that deployers can interpret the system's output. EU AI Act Article 68 gives affected persons the right to lodge complaints and receive explanations from deployers. At Delper's scale, these are not abstract rights — they apply concretely to wallet freezes, KYC rejections, food allocation changes, and city service decisions affecting 6 billion people.

GDPR Article 22 — Automated Decision-Making Safeguards

✓  No solely automated significant decisions: Agents 1, 3, and 5 make or inform decisions that significantly affect individuals (financial access, KYC, wallet). GDPR Art. 22 requires that these decisions are not taken solely by automated means without the right to human intervention. Delper's Agent Permission Matrix already requires human confirmation above defined thresholds. Below those thresholds, the right to request human review (documented above) satisfies Art. 22(3).

✓  Profiling transparency: Where agent outputs constitute profiling of individuals under GDPR Art. 4(4), Delper's privacy notice (to be published pre-IPO) must disclose: (a) that profiling occurs; (b) the logic involved; (c) the significance and envisaged consequences for the data subject.

✓  Children: Any resident or user identified as under 16 (or the applicable age in their jurisdiction) must not be subject to automated profiling without parental consent. Agent 3 KYC age verification must flag under-16 accounts for manual processing only.

MAS FEAT — Additional Singapore-Specific Requirements

✓  MAS Technology Risk Guidelines (TRM 2021): Agents 1, 5, and 7 constitute critical AI applications under MAS TRM 2021 definitions (material financial transactions, risk management). Delper must maintain an AI system inventory submitted to MAS annually from Year 4 (IPO), documenting all AI systems used in financial decision-making, their risk classification, and governance controls.

✓  MAS Notice FAA-N16 / SFA 04-N02: Where Agent 7 treasury outputs or Agent 1 AML decisions constitute actions regulated under the Financial Advisers Act or Securities and Futures Act, human licensed adviser or compliance officer must be the named decision-maker of record. AI output is the draft; licensed human is the signatory.

✓  MAS outsourcing guidelines (MAS Guidelines on Outsourcing, 2016): Anthropic's Claude API constitutes a material outsourced AI service. Delper must maintain a vendor management framework for Anthropic as a critical vendor — including SLA monitoring, right to audit, business continuity planning, and documented exit strategy if Anthropic's API becomes unavailable. v5 FINANCING MECHANICS: (1) IPO proceeds ($15T Y4) and all 9 FPO tranches ($15T each, Y5–Y13 = $135T) are ring-fenced exclusively for CapEx and Gold purchases — not for OpEx. (2) Total CapEx+Gold Y5–Y21 = $368.88T; less IPO+FPO $150T = structural gap $218.88T, distributed equally across 17 years = $12.88T/yr. (3) Each year's SBLC = (CapEx+Gold needed) − (IPO/FPO applied this year). Y12 and Y13: FPO ($15T) exceeds CapEx+Gold ($7.66B and $8.28B) so SBLC = zero; FPO surplus flows to ops. Post-Y13 (no more FPO): gold purchase only, SBLC covers it. (4) Operating profit from prior year carried forward to next year's ops pool. Y1→Y4 trade BF of $413.95T funds operational expenses throughout construction phase. (5) SBLC type: MT760 First-Demand Irrevocable · ICC UCP 600 · Called by independent trustee against verified CapEx milestone. (6) Amazon AI Cloud (AWS) serves as the fully managed cloud backbone, replacing all on-premises physical infrastructure with scalable Amazon AI Cloud OpEx. Quantum Computer = standalone CapEx from Y5. All CapEx zero Y0–Y4.

Comprehensive DSCR Module - 5 Levels · All 21 Years · NOI / Total Debt Service

Benchmark: Commercial >= 1.25x · Preferred >= 1.50x
Standard DSCR Formula
DSCR = Net Operating Income (NOI) / Total Debt Service (TDS)
NOI = Revenue - Operating Expenses
Corporate: EBITDA (Gross Revenue - Op Costs)
Smart City: Rental Revenue - 15% City OPEX
Retrofit: Yield Revenue - 30% OPEX
TDS = Annual Principal + Interest
Corporate: ESG Int + MTN Int + MTN Retirement
Smart City: SBLC Interest + SBLC Principal/25yr
Retrofit: MTN Interest (reducing) + $153,300/yr

Debt Payoff — 5yr Window · 1.5yr Settling · Reinvestment Cascade

Rule: Each smart city has a 5-year debt payoff window from its completion date. The first 1.5 years is an initial settling period — no payoff contribution. Active repayment runs for 3.5 years (42 months) at $80B/city/month profit. Once a city clears its own proportional debt share ($606B in 7.6 months), its remaining 34.4 months of surplus profit is reinvested into the collective debt pool, accelerating payoff for all remaining cities.

Key Insight: The $2,112T annual profit from 4.4 billion workers is 1.59× the entire $1,332.41T debt stack. Even at 20% allocation, the debt is cleared before Year 19. With full reinvestment, the cascade effect (each city clearing own share then pooling surplus) compresses payoff to Year 16.1 — leaving $6,059.59T in free surplus capital for further city expansion, humanitarian programmes, and token buybacks.
